content: 1. Individuals at particularly high risk of contracting multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) require prompt evaluation and, if necessary, immediate treatment to mitigate the risk of disease progression and transmission. For further details on managing drug-resistant TB in children, refer to Chapter 7. 2. Contact investigation is strongly recommended for household and close contacts of index cases with the following characteristics: sputum smear-positive pulmonary TB, confirmed or suspected MDR-TB or extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB), individuals living with HIV, or children under 5 years of age. This recommendation is based on very low-quality evidence but is strongly endorsed. 3. In resource-limited settings, priority should be given to screening contacts of sputum smear-positive TB cases, as these individuals are the most likely to transmit the infection. National tuberculosis programs (NTPs) may choose to include contacts of all TB index cases for screening, depending on available resources. 4. In some settings, screening of child contacts includes tuberculin skin testing (TST) to detect infection and chest X-rays (CXR) to identify disease. However, routine assessment of exposed contacts does not necessarily require TST or CXR, as these tests may not be readily available or feasible in lowand middle-income settings. Clinical assessment alone is often sufficient to determine whether a contact is symptomatic or well. 5. A symptom-based approach to screening allows health workers at peripheral levels to conduct evaluations without requiring access to district-level health facilities. Only symptomatic contacts need to be referred to secondary-level facilities for further assessment. 6. Recent research indicates that symptom-based screening for child TB contacts is both safe and more feasible than diagnostic test-based approaches in resource-limited settings. This strategy is effective for managing contacts and reducing the burden of TB in children. 7. Children under 5 years of age who are household or close contacts of TB patients and who, after appropriate evaluation, are found not to have TB disease should receive six months of isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) at a dose of 10 mg/kg per day (range: 7–15 mg/kg, maximum dose: 300 mg/day). This is a strong recommendation supported by high-quality evidence. 8. Preventive therapy is indicated for asymptomatic contacts or those in whom TB disease has been excluded, particularly if the contact is under 5 years of age or living with HIV, regardless of age. This therapy significantly reduces the likelihood of developing TB disease during childhood. 9. While referred to as preventive therapy, IPT is essentially treatment for latent TB infection. The standard regimen involves daily isoniazid for six months. Single isoniazid dispersible tablets (100 mg) are available through the Global Drug Facility (GDF). 10. Follow-up for children receiving IPT should occur at least every two months until treatment is completed. There is no risk of isoniazid resistance developing in children receiving IPT, even if active TB is inadvertently missed. 11. In high HIV-prevalence settings, TB contact investigations provide an opportunity to screen for both TB and HIV. Determining the HIV status of the source case and offering HIV counseling and testing to contacts is crucial. 12. All household and close contacts of TB patients in high HIV-prevalence settings should be counseled and tested for HIV. This is a strong recommendation, albeit based on very low-quality evidence. 13. In low HIV-prevalence settings, household and close contacts of TB patients with symptoms suggestive of TB disease may be offered HIV counseling and testing as part of their clinical evaluation. This is a conditional recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. 14. All household contacts of an index case who is a person living with HIV (PLHIV) should be counseled and tested for HIV. This is a strong recommendation supported by very low-quality evidence. 15. Contact screening and management are recommended by most NTPs but are rarely implemented in lowand middle-income settings where the majority of childhood TB cases occur. There is no need to establish separate infrastructure for contact management; existing NTP structures and specialist support can be utilized. 16. A symptom-based screening approach enables contact management at the community level without requiring additional resources. Written guidelines and standardized protocols should be developed and followed to improve the efficiency and uniformity of contact investigations. 17. Infection control measures are essential to prevent TB transmission in healthcare facilities, congregate settings, and households. These measures should be integrated into patient-centered approaches and supported by community advocacy to reduce stigma and promote sustainable behavior change. 18. TB infection control guidelines published by WHO emphasize reducing transmission risks in healthcare facilities, congregate settings, and households. These guidelines prioritize infection control measures based on the burden of TB, HIV, and MDR-TB at the national level. 19. Effective TB infection control requires actions such as safe sputum collection, promoting cough hygiene, triaging presumptive TB cases, ensuring rapid diagnosis and treatment, improving ventilation, protecting healthcare workers, and monitoring infection control practices. 20. Nosocomial TB transmission in high-burden settings is often exacerbated by factors such as poor ventilation, overcrowding, and lack of administrative measures. Addressing these issues is critical to reducing transmission risks. 21. Children are particularly vulnerable to TB transmission in healthcare settings, especially infants and young children living with HIV. Infection control measures should be implemented in all areas where sick children are seen, including neonatal care units, HIV clinics, and facilities for malnourished children. 22. Children with smear-positive TB should be isolated to prevent transmission. In congregate settings such as schools, childcare facilities, and refugee camps, measures should be taken to minimize the risk of TB exposure. 23. The clinical presentation of TB in children often overlaps with other conditions such as pneumonia, HIV, and malnutrition, making infection control measures relevant across all pediatric healthcare settings.
